html:
The Lex Claudia was a Roman law of 218 BCE that barred senators and their sons from owning large seagoing ships. A ship could hold no more than 300 amphoras, enough to carry produce from their own estates but not to trade at sea.

It was proposed by the tribune Quintus Claudius at the start of the Second Punic War. According to Livy, only one senator backed it: Gaius Flaminius, builder of the Via Flaminia. The rest of the Senate hated it. The thinking behind it was that trade for profit was beneath a senator.

The effect was lasting. Senators put their wealth into land, which became the respectable form of riches in Rome. Sea trade and the big state contracts for supplies, building and tax collecting went to the equites, the rich men just below the Senate. They grew into a wealthy business class that later clashed with senators over control of the courts and the provinces. The goods they carried included the oil and wine shipped in amphoras.
sum: The Lex Claudia was a Roman law of 218 BCE that barred senators and their sons from owning large seagoing ships. A ship could hold no more than 300 amphoras, enough to carry produce from their own estates but not to trade at sea.
